notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Matthew 19 from the sources I was able to consult. I indicate in brackets where searches were limited and certain denominational perspectives could not be retrieved.

---

## Matthew 19 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### vv. 1–2: Jesus Departs Galilee for Judea Beyond the Jordan

**v. 1:** Matthew’s formula “when Jesus had finished these sayings” closes the discourse of chapter 18 and marks a major narrative turn: Jesus now leaves Galilee for the final time before the crucifixion, heading toward Jerusalem via Peraea (the region east of the Jordan). Ellicott notes this verse covers a “considerable interval of time” filled in by Luke’s Peraean ministry (Luke 9:51–18:30) and John’s accounts of visits to Jerusalem for Tabernacles and Dedication (John 7:2; 10:22). The Pulpit Commentary explains that “beyond Jordan” belongs to the verb “came” — Jesus took the longer but safer route through Peraea rather than direct through Samaria. Gill concurs that Jesus “came into the coasts of Judea beyond Jordan,” i.e., the country bordering Judea on this side (or east) of the Jordan. Precept Austin notes this was Herod Antipas’s territory — the very ruler who had beheaded John the Baptist over the issue of divorce — which sets the stage for the Pharisees’ trap.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/19.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/matthew/19.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-19-commentary

**v. 2:** Large crowds followed, and Jesus healed them. Precept Austin highlights the verb “followed” (*akoloutheō*), noting that in context these were largely superficial followers — “the text saith He healed them, but it saith not, they believed in him” (Poole). Clarke adds: “Some to be instructed — some to be healed — some through curiosity — and some to ensnare him.” Mark’s parallel notes Jesus also taught them (Mark 10:1).
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-19-commentary
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/

---

### vv. 3–9: The Pharisees’ Test on Divorce

**v. 3:** The Pharisees came “testing Him” — not with honest inquiry but seeking to trap Him. The question, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?”, was a live controversy between the schools of Shammai (strict: only for sexual immorality) and Hillel (lax: for almost any cause, including spoiling dinner). Ellicott and Pulpit both detail that the Pharisees hoped to force Jesus to alienate either the popular majority (if He sided with Shammai) or the stricter moralists (if He sided with Hillel). They may also have hoped Jesus would, like John the Baptist, say something to provoke Herod Antipas. Enduring Word (citing Carson) notes that the Pharisees possibly “hoped that Jesus would say something that would entangle him in the Herod-Herodias affair so that he might meet the Baptist’s fate.”
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/matthew/19.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/19.htm

**v. 4:** Jesus bypasses the rabbinic debate entirely and appeals to Scripture itself: “Have you not read…?” He quotes Genesis 1:27 — “He who made them at the beginning made them male and female.” Enduring Word says Jesus “asserts God’s authority over marriage; it is God’s institution, not man’s — so it is fair to say that His rules apply.” Spurgeon remarks: “Our Lord honors Holy Scripture by drawing his argument therefrom. He chose specially to set his seal upon a part of the story of creation — that story which modern critics speak of as if it were fable or myth.” The Pulpit Commentary notes that God made the first humans “a male and a female, not a male and females” — leaving no room for polygamy or easy divorce in the original design.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/matthew/19.htm

**v. 5:** Jesus quotes Genesis 2:24: a man shall leave father and mother, be joined (literally “glued,” *proskollēthēsetai*) to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh. Ellicott notes that while these words appear in Genesis as Adam’s, they were “prompted by the Holy Spirit, and stamped with the divine sanction,” so they function as a divine oracle. Enduring Word emphasises that this one-flesh union prohibits polygamy and is “both a fact (they are…one flesh) and a goal (shall become one flesh).”
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/19.htm

**v. 6:** “So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate.” The Pulpit Commentary argues that this declares the indissolubility of marriage: “His hearers plainly understood him so to speak, as we see from the objection which they urged.” Enduring Word notes that marriage “is not merely a social contract” — God has joined, and man must honour what God has joined. Clarke observes that the Greek word for “joined together” (*sunezeuxen*) means “yoked together, as oxen in the plough, where each must pull equally.”
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/matthew/19.htm

**v. 7:** The Pharisees counter: “Why then did Moses command to give a certificate of divorce?” They misrepresent Deuteronomy 24:1. As Enduring Word notes, Jesus “noted the difference between ‘command’ and ‘permitted.’ God never commands divorce, but He does permit it.” Spurgeon says: “Every reader of the passage in the books of Moses…will be struck with the Pharisees’ unfair rendering of it.” The Mosaic regulation was about *controlling* an already-existing practice, not creating or promoting divorce.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-19-commentary

**v. 8:** Jesus says Moses “permitted” (not commanded) divorce “because of the hardness of your hearts, but from the beginning it was not so.” Ellicott explains that the Law’s concession was a “step backwards when compared with the primary law of nature,” made necessary because the people had sunk so low that the higher ideal was practically impossible. “But for the possibility of divorce the wife would have been the victim of the husband’s tyranny.” Enduring Word (citing France) says: “The thought is not so much of the cruelty of men to their wives, as of their unresponsiveness to the mind and will of God.”
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/19.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/

**v. 9:** “Whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery.” Enduring Word (citing Carson) notes that the Greek *porneia* is broad, “covering a wide span of sexual impropriety” and “should not be restricted unless the context requires it.” Enduring Word also adds the case of abandonment by an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:15) as a second biblical ground. The Pulpit Commentary engages in a long discussion of whether the exceptive clause permits remarriage. It argues that the phrase “whoso marrieth her which is put away doth commit adultery” shows the marriage bond remains — if she were truly free, marrying her would not be adultery. Therefore, “divorce in such a case does not destroy the *vinculum matrimonii*, the marriage bond.” However, the Pulpit acknowledges that many theologians and civil laws interpret it differently.

**Denominational Differences on v. 9:**
- **Catholic view:** The Catholic Encyclopedia states that Catholic theology “has always maintained” that Matthew’s exceptive clause permits separation (*divortium a mensa et toro*) but never remarriage while the spouse lives. The clause “except it be for fornication” modifies only the putting-away, not the remarriage. The Catholic position is that marriage is absolutely indissoluble once consummated, based on harmonising Matthew with Mark, Luke, and Paul, who give no exception. — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/05054c.htm
- **Orthodox view:** According to Catholic Answers, the modern Orthodox churches permit divorce and remarriage in certain cases, drawing on later Byzantine civil law (Emperor Justinian’s code) rather than strictly on the New Testament. However, the earliest ante-Nicene fathers (Hermas, Athenagoras, Clement, Origen) uniformly forbade remarriage after divorce while the spouse lived. — https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/east-vs-west-divorce-remarriage
- **Protestant evangelical view (Enduring Word, charismatic/Pentecostal):** Divorce and remarriage are permitted on the grounds of *porneia* (sexual immorality) and abandonment by an unbeliever (1 Cor. 7:15). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/
- *Note: Baptist (DesiringGod/Piper), Lutheran (LCMS), Reformed (Ligonier), Methodist/Wesleyan, and Anglican perspectives could not be individually retrieved due to search limits.*

---

### vv. 10–12: The Disciples’ Reaction and Jesus on Celibacy

**v. 10:** The disciples react: “If this is the case…it is better not to marry.” Ellicott notes this reflects the popularity of Hillel’s lax view even among the disciples. They saw marriage without easy escape as a burden. Enduring Word (citing Trapp) comments: “It is not evil to marry, but good to be wary; to look ere one leap.”
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/19.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/

**v. 11:** Jesus replies: “Not everyone can accept this word, but only those to whom it has been given.” Ellicott explains that “this saying” refers to the disciples’ comment that “it is not good to marry.” Jesus declares that judgment false for most; celibacy is a gift, not a universal rule. The Pulpit clarifies: “Christ passes over these ignoble scruples, and enunciates the only principle which should lead a man to abstain from marriage.”
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/19.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/matthew/19.htm

**v. 12:** Three kinds of eunuchs: (1) those born without capacity for marriage; (2) those made so by men (castration, common in the ancient East); (3) those who “have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake” — voluntary celibacy for spiritual service. Ellicott stresses that the celibacy of mere “self-indulgence, or even of selfish prudence, tends but too fatally to impurity.” It must be “for the kingdom of heaven’s sake” — to enlarge its range and bring souls to Christ. Spurgeon adds: “Some have but feeble desires concerning marriage, and they were so born…Abstinence from marriage is to a few a choice gift, answering high purposes; but to the many, marriage is as necessary as it is honorable.”
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/19.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-19-commentary

---

### vv. 13–15: Jesus Blesses Little Children

**v. 13:** Little children (Luke 18:15 uses *brephē*, infants) were brought for Jesus to place hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuked those bringing them. Ellicott suggests the disciples may have thought, after Jesus’ teaching on the “eunuch” life, that children were a distraction from higher spiritual concerns. Enduring Word notes it was a Jewish custom to bring children to elders for blessing on the Day of Atonement eve.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/19.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/

**v. 14:** “Let the little children come to Me…for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.” Mark adds that Jesus was “much displeased” (Mark 10:14). Ellicott says His “tenderness of sympathy was kindled into indignation at the rough indifference of the disciples.” The kingdom belongs to those with childlike humility and trust.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/19.htm

**v. 15:** Jesus laid hands on them and departed. Ellicott notes this has “rightly been regarded…as the true warrant for infant baptism” — if infants were capable of receiving spiritual blessing then, why not now? Mark records Jesus “folded them in His arms” as well (Mark 10:16).
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/19.htm

---

### vv. 16–22: The Rich Young Ruler

**v. 16:** A man (Matthew: “young man,” v.20; Luke 18:18: “ruler”; Mark 10:17: he “ran” and “knelt”) asks, “Teacher, what good thing must I do to obtain eternal life?” Ellicott notes he uses the address “Good Master” (in Mark and Luke; the better MSS of Matthew omit “good”). Ellicott comments: “The question exhibits the highest and noblest phase of Pharisaism” — sincere, earnest, believing eternal life could be won “by some one good deed of exceptional and heroic goodness.”
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/19.htm

**v. 17:** Jesus responds, “Why do you ask Me about what is good? There is only One who is good. If you want to enter life, keep the commandments.” Spurgeon explains: “The argument is clear: either Jesus was good, or he ought not to have called him good; but as there is none good but God, Jesus who is good must be God.” GotQuestions explains that Jesus was not teaching salvation by works; rather, He “was emphasizing the Law as God’s perfect standard. If you can keep the Law perfectly, then you can escape sin’s penalty — but that’s a big if.”
- https://www.gotquestions.org/rich-young-ruler.html
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-19-commentary

**vv. 18–19:** The man asks “Which ones?” Jesus lists the second table of the Decalogue: murder, adultery, theft, false witness, honour parents, and “love your neighbour as yourself.” Ellicott notes that Jesus listed those commands the young man would consider “the mere commonplaces of morality” — precisely to expose that he had not, in fact, kept them. Spurgeon: “The last-quoted command summarized the rest, and it ought to have opened the questioner’s eyes to his shortcomings; for who has loved his neighbor as himself?”
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/19.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-19-commentary

**v. 20:** The young man claims, “All these I have kept from my youth. What do I still lack?” GotQuestions calls this “a key statement. The young man was obviously religious and sincere…His problem was that he considered himself to be faultless concerning the Law.” Jesus will now challenge that self-assessment.
- https://www.gotquestions.org/rich-young-ruler.html

**v. 21:** “If you want to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor…Then come, follow Me.” Enduring Word says “the call to forsake everything and follow Jesus is a call to put God first in all things. It is full obedience to the first table of the law, which dealt with a man’s relation to God.” The man had kept the external, horizontal commands but failed at the first and greatest — loving God with all his heart. His wealth was his true god.

**Modern Debate — Prosperity/Word of Faith:** GotQuestions explains that prosperity gospel teachers “see the Holy Spirit as a power to be put to use for whatever the believer wills,” teaching that “faith is a formula by which we manipulate the spiritual laws.” This directly contradicts passages like Matthew 19:21–24, where Jesus calls a wealthy man to give everything away and warns that wealth is a spiritual danger, not a sign of blessing. “If riches were a reasonable goal for the godly, Jesus would have pursued it. But He did not, preferring instead to have no place to lay His head (Matthew 8:20).”
- https://www.gotquestions.org/prosperity-gospel.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/

**v. 22:** The young man “went away in sorrow, because he had great wealth.” Enduring Word notes this shows his idol was exposed. Mark 10:21 adds that Jesus, “looking at him, loved him.” The call to sell everything was an act of love meant to free him.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/

---

### vv. 23–26: The Danger of Riches

**v. 23:** “Truly I tell you, it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.” Enduring Word explains that wealth breeds false independence and blinds us to our need for God. GotQuestions adds: “Material wealth can also lead to complacency. The Laodicean church claimed, ‘I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing,’ but they were ‘wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked’ (Revelation 3:17).”
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/
- https://www.gotquestions.org/hard-for-a-rich-man-to-enter-the-kingdom.html

**v. 24:** “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.” Enduring Word says this “is meant to be humorous and impossible-sounding,” illustrating the sheer impossibility from a human standpoint. Some popular interpretations suggest “eye of a needle” was a small gate in Jerusalem’s wall, but Enduring Word does not endorse that view — the point is the impossibility. The Pulpit Commentary takes the hyperbolic reading at face value: an utterly impossible thing for man.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/

**v. 25:** The disciples are “greatly astonished” and ask, “Who then can be saved?” In Jewish thought, wealth was often seen as a sign of God’s blessing; if the blessed cannot enter, who can?
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/

**v. 26:** “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” Jesus affirms that salvation — for rich or poor — is a work of God’s grace, not human effort. Enduring Word: the point is not that riches make salvation harder for God, but that God must do what man cannot.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/

---

### vv. 27–30: Peter’s Question about Rewards

**v. 27:** Peter says, “We have left everything to follow You. What then will there be for us?” Enduring Word calls this “Peter’s blunt question.” Unlike the rich young ruler, the disciples *had* left everything. Peter’s question, though perhaps self-interested, is honest.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/

**v. 28:** Jesus promises that “in the renewal of all things (*palingenesia*, regeneration), when the Son of Man sits on His glorious throne, you who have followed Me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” Enduring Word sees this as a millennial promise — the disciples will have a special role in the Messianic kingdom. The “renewal” refers to the future restoration of all creation.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/

**v. 29:** “Everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or wife or children or fields for My name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life.” Enduring Word stresses that the “hundredfold” is not primarily material — “we can’t receive a hundred wives” — but spiritual: joy, peace, contentment, the family of God, and the supplying of genuine needs. Jesus is not promising earthly riches.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/

**v. 30:** “But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.” This proverb-like saying bookends the rich young ruler story and introduces the parable of the workers in the vineyard (Matthew 20:1–16). Spurgeon: “Our King is here seen arranging human positions as they appear from his throne. To his eye, many first are last, and many last are first; and he will in his kingdom place men according to the divine order.” The rich young ruler seemed “first” in human terms but went away unable to enter; the disciples seemed “last” but will reign with Christ.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-19/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-19-commentary
